To recognise the form instantly from its ending and to announce big news in Japanese.

Mid-November, Sunday, ten in the morning in Bucharest. Mihai has called everyone into one single video call: Kenji and Mrs Suzuki (with Tama) from Madrid, where it’s nine; Haruka and Sakura from Hiroshima, Mrs Fumiko from Kyoto and Yuki from Tokyo, where it’s five in the afternoon. Ana is sitting down, as usual; on screen you can only see her face.
Can everyone hear me? Mihai summoned me, and look — nine o’clock on a Sunday morning and I’m made to sit in front of the computer.
I’m here from Tokyo. Mrs Fumiko, it’s been so long!
Yuki, you look well. Oh, I can see my sister and Tama too.
Tama, say hello nicely. …Oh dear, she ran off on me.
Mihai, hurry up! I was told you have something important to say today.
Yes. Actually… Ana, could you stand up for a moment?
Oh my! Ana, could it be…
Yes. We’re expecting a baby. The due date is the fifteenth of January.
Whaaat?! January?! That’s only two months away!
Why didn’t you tell us until now?! I’ve been fooled all this time!
I’m sorry. I kept it hidden until the move had settled down, so I could surprise you all at once.
(Crying) Oh my, oh my… Please don’t make an old woman cry.
Sister, here’s a handkerchief. …They made me cry too.
Oh, so that’s why you turned down the beer at Kenji’s restaurant, Ana!
And that’s why Mihai was making you drink milk every evening!
(Laughing) As a doctor, I make sure she eats and sleeps properly.
Ana, take good care of yourself. Let me send you something from Japan.
Mum, let me choose the baby’s clothes!
Thank you, Sakura. …And one more thing. It’s a girl.
A girl?! Then she’s my little sister! I’m going to be a big sister!

“nomasarete ita” = you were made to drink
nin-shin: two “n”s that sound on their own, each as long as a full syllable. Don’t swallow them: ni-n-shi-n.
i-chi-ga-tsu juu-go-ni-chi: the “u” in つ is almost silent, the “u” in じゅう is long. Japanese dates have special readings: ついたち (1st), はつか (20th).
sa-re-ru / sa-se-ra-re-ru: when people talk fast, listen for a “se” in the middle. No “se”: passive; with “se”: causative(-passive).
The subject RECEIVES the action; the one who does it takes に. Form: godan a-column + れる, ichidan る → られる, する → される, くる → こられる.
Mihai was praised by Dr Ionescu.
I was told there was important news.
When someone does something DIRECTLY TO YOU, Japanese prefers the passive: ミハイ に よばれた (I was called by Mihai) sounds more natural than ミハイ が わたし を よんだ.

Same form, but the subject is the person AFFECTED (usually unpleasantly), even when the verb has no object. English says things like “it rained on me”, “my cat ran off on me”, “I had my wallet stolen”.
my cat ran off on me
With ～ちゃう (ch. 26) the annoyance grows: タマ に にげられちゃった = oh no, Tama ran off on me.

Someone MAKES or LETS someone else do something: godan a-column + せる, ichidan る → させる, する → させる, くる → こさせる. The person made to act takes に if the verb already has an object with を; with verbs that have no object, it usually takes を.
To ask permission: ～させて ください (polite, ch. 33). Among people who are close, ～させて is enough: あかちゃん の ふく を えらばせて! = let me choose the baby clothes!
New: ちょうだい = a casual “please”, the warm version of ください, used mostly by women and with children or people you’re close to. ～させて ちょうだい = let me…; ～ないで ちょうだい = please don’t…: としより を なかせないで ちょうだい.
You are MADE to do something you didn’t want to do: ～させられる (long) or, with godan verbs not ending in す, ～される (short). The one who makes you do it takes に.
Nine o’clock on a Sunday morning and I’m made to sit in front of the computer.
I was made to drink milk by Mihai.
なかされる and かんがえさせられる often have a nice meaning: a story moved you to tears, a film made you think.

After the call, Ana’s phone didn’t stop buzzing all day.
Kenji: Congratulations! It bugs me that Mihai fooled me, but I’m so happy! I’ll make the baby’s ramen myself.

After the call, another message came from Sakura: “Ana, and how did you tell Mihai? Tell me everything!”
Ana looked at the little wooden box on the shelf and smiled. The story takes us back to the end of the honeymoon.
In the last week in the village in the Carpathians, one morning, the smell of milk made Ana feel sick.
Mihai, worried, took her pulse and took her temperature. But she had no fever.
“I’m just tired,” Ana said. But Ana had a little suspicion.
That afternoon, the two of them went to the market in the little town in the cart pulled by Sura.
The road was full of potholes and, every time the cart jolted, Ana held on to Mihai’s arm.
“Are you okay? Let’s take it slow today.” Mihai called out to Sura and made her slow down a little.
While Mihai was buying the bread and salt Grandpa had asked for, Ana went into a pharmacy on her own.
The next morning, Ana got up while it was still dark and stared at the small test.
Two lines. However many times she looked, there were still two.
Looking at the mountains beyond the window, Ana couldn’t move for a while. She was happy, she was scared, and she was close to tears.
She thought about waking Mihai right away. But she changed her mind. She wanted to give him this news in a special way.
The day before, at the market, Ana had stopped in front of an old woman’s stall.
The old woman, it seems, knitted socks by hand during the long winter nights.
Among lots of big socks there was just one tiny pair of white socks, no bigger than a finger.
For some reason, Ana couldn’t take her eyes off them. And she had bought them secretly, so Mihai wouldn’t see.
Ana called out to Grandpa in the kitchen: “Grandpa, do you have a little box?”
Without asking anything, Grandpa took a wooden box out from the back of the wardrobe for her.
It was a box Grandpa had carved long ago for Ileana. Little flowers were carved on the lid.
Grandpa looked closely at Ana’s face and smiled a little. It seemed he had realised something.
That evening, in front of the stove, Ana gave Mihai the box. “A present. Open it.”
Mihai sat down on his little stool from childhood and opened the box. Inside were the tiny white socks.
Ana took his hand and gently placed it on her tummy. “They belong to someone who’s coming in January.”
Mihai was silent for a while. With his doctor’s brain, he worked out the due date on the spot.
Then, suddenly, his eyes turned red. His big hands were trembling.
“When did you find out?” “This morning. While it was still dark. I thought about waking you, but I wanted to put it in this box before giving it to you.”
Mihai hugged Ana and cried like a child. And it made Ana cry too.
From the next room came Grandpa’s voice. In Romanian, as if he were talking to himself.
“Ileana, did you hear? It’s a great-grandchild.”
Just then, the old door quietly swung open in the wind. Mihai and Ana looked at each other and laughed.
The next morning, without saying a word, Grandpa swapped Ana’s milk for a warm tea.
And when they said goodbye, he held Ana’s hand and spoke to her for a long time in Romanian. Mihai translated.
“Take care of yourself. Even if someone makes you do too much, say no. Next time, come with the great-grandchild.”
When they got back to Madrid, the first people they told were just the two mothers.
Elena shouted: “I knew it!” That’s why she had said it would be better for the flat in Bucharest to have two rooms.
Carmen cried the whole time on the other end of the line and couldn’t say a thing until the very end.
But Ana really wanted to tell “the Japanese family” in her own words, all of them together. So she waited until the move had settled down.
Even after they came to Bucharest, during video calls Ana always sat down and showed only her face. There were days she hid under a blanket too.
Mihai, “as a doctor”, so Ana wouldn’t overdo it, made her go to bed early every evening and drink milk.
“I want to give Sakura the biggest surprise of all.” Ana kept saying that.
And today, in the call where everyone had gathered, that day had really, finally come.
Ana wrote Sakura a long message and at the end added this:
“The socks are still on the shelf in Bucharest. Next to your photo.”
The reply came straight away: “Your story made me cry again. I’m going to learn to knit from Mum and knit another pair of socks myself!”
Ana put the phone down and laughed. Just then, inside her tummy, the baby gave a kick.
“See, it’s from your big sister.” When Ana said that, the baby kicked once more, nice and strong.
